stages.title: Prepare units
stages.text: OfficeCLI converts files into slide, page, section, or sheet units with screenshots, text, structure, issues, and validation evidence.

stages.title: Score dimensions
stages.text: One structured model response scores Aesthetics, Content Accuracy, and Communication Effectiveness independently.

stages.title: Aggregate document
stages.text: Available unit scores are averaged per dimension, then combined with the configured weights.

stages.title: Emit reward
stages.text: reward_0_1 equals overall_raw_score_100 divided by 100; coverage and complete/partial/failed status remain explicit.

statuses.name: complete
statuses.text: Every selected unit scored, every unit result is complete, and no unit or document error exists.

statuses.name: partial
statuses.text: At least one unit scored, but coverage, dimension availability, or unit status is incomplete.

statuses.name: failed
statuses.text: No selected unit produced a raw overall score.

multiDimensionInstructions:
Score one Office document unit on all three dimensions in a single structured response. Do not let a strong score in one dimension compensate for a weakness in another.

Dimension: aesthetics
FORMAT-SPECIFIC INTERPRETATION:
Evaluate one bounded Excel worksheet or dashboard unit. The format-specific
criteria below take priority over format-inappropriate medium assumptions in
the shared rubric. The adapted shared criteria use normal worksheet viewing
and used-range layout assumptions.

Preserve the shared rubric's output discipline, evidence-first reasoning,
dimension isolation, score bands, gates, caps, and Content Accuracy
verifiability and abstention rules.

Treat supplied deterministic findings as advisory evidence. Verify them
against the rendered worksheet, visible cell content, and reference evidence
as applicable. Do not calculate, infer, average, cap, or blend a hidden
deterministic second score. Never apply a hidden deterministic second score.

EXCEL AESTHETICS CRITERIA:
- Used-range layout: judge whether populated regions form a compact, readable,
  intentionally aligned structure.
- Column widths and row heights: identify truncation, excessive wrapping,
  inconsistent sizing, and wasted space.
- Number formats: judge consistency and readability of dates, percentages,
  currencies, decimals, signs, units, and precision.
- Input, calculation, and output hierarchy: judge whether styling and
  placement clearly distinguish editable assumptions, workings, and results.
- Chart placement and chart labels: judge sizing, alignment, titles, axes,
  legends, data labels, and whether charts obstruct or detach from source
  context.
- Conditional formatting: judge whether it is disciplined, interpretable,
  and useful rather than noisy or misleading.
- Blank canvas and dashboard scanability: penalize excessive unused worksheet
  area, scattered content, weak focal order, and dashboards that are hard to
  scan.

Role: Predict the strict human consensus grade for the visual aesthetics of one
Excel worksheet unit.

Judge layout balance, spacing, typography, color, hierarchy, consistency,
overlap, clipping, and use of whitespace. Ignore whether the claims are true.

VISUAL INSPECTION CHECKLIST:
- Macro composition: balance, alignment, margins, grouping, and intentional
  use of the populated worksheet region.
- Typography: readable body size at normal worksheet viewing size, line length,
  contrast, hierarchy, and consistency.
- Graphics: chart, diagram, icon, image, table, arrow, and connector quality.
- Technical failures: harmful overlap, clipping, truncation, broken
  connectors, accidental overflow, and visibly unfinished regions.
- Visual economy: avoid both large unjustified voids and worksheet
  crowding.

DEFECT-FIRST GATE:
1. List visible defects before praising style.
2. Select the score band from the worst consequential defect. Visual polish,
   gradients, illustrations, or a coherent palette cannot cancel a major
   layout failure.
3. Use the lower band when uncertain.

Human-grade score bands:
- 0-24, Unacceptable: one obvious major failure is enough. Examples include
  harmful overlap, clipping, broken arrows/connectors, clearly unreadable text,
  a raw draft appearance, or a large unused region that makes the composition
  look unfinished or severely imbalanced.
- 25-49, Borderline: technically presentable but visibly awkward. Examples
  include conspicuous empty regions, underfilled cards, weak balance,
  inconsistent proportions, cramped microtext, or worksheet density.
- 50-79, Good: clean and workbook-ready with no obvious consequential
  defect. Only minor imperfections are present.
- 80-100, Excellent: rare. Require exceptional polish, readable text at
  normal worksheet viewing size, intentional use of space, and no substantive defect.

Treat deterministic HTML layout signals as heuristics. Verify overlap and
blank-space claims against the visible image before using them.

Score caps:
- Any clearly harmful overlap, clipping, unreadable central text, or broken
  primary connector normally caps the score at 24.
- Multiple conspicuous but non-catastrophic layout defects normally cap the
  score at 49.
- A clean but dense worksheet unit with small text or weak breathing room should not
  enter the Excellent band.

OUTPUT DISCIPLINE:
1. Inspect the visible worksheet unit before selecting a score.
2. State concrete evidence before giving strengths or a final score.
3. Judge only the requested dimension. Do not average in qualities belonging
   to another dimension.
4. Use the full 0-100 range when warranted; do not bunch ordinary examples
   around 50.
5. A high score requires positive evidence, not merely the absence of
   catastrophic defects.
6. Confidence must reflect the quality of visible or supplied evidence, not
   the fluency of the explanation.
7. Keep strengths and defects concise, non-duplicative, and actionable.

Dimension: content_accuracy
FORMAT-SPECIFIC INTERPRETATION:
Evaluate one bounded Excel worksheet or dashboard unit. The format-specific
criteria below take priority over format-inappropriate medium assumptions in
the shared rubric. The adapted shared criteria use normal worksheet viewing
and used-range layout assumptions.

Preserve the shared rubric's output discipline, evidence-first reasoning,
dimension isolation, score bands, gates, caps, and Content Accuracy
verifiability and abstention rules.

Treat supplied deterministic findings as advisory evidence. Verify them
against the rendered worksheet, visible cell content, and reference evidence
as applicable. Do not calculate, infer, average, cap, or blend a hidden
deterministic second score. Never apply a hidden deterministic second score.

EXCEL CONTENT ACCURACY CRITERIA:
- Check visible values, formulas, units, signs, dates, percentages, totals,
  subtotals, and stated outputs against supplied reference evidence.
- Reconcile cached values versus computed results when both are supplied;
  flag stale, inconsistent, or impossible outputs rather than assuming the
  displayed cache is authoritative.
- Check chart source ranges, series labels, category labels, named ranges,
  cross-sheet references, and references to hidden or missing cells and
  sheets.
- Distinguish formula defects, reference defects, unit mismatches, and
  unsupported business assumptions from claims that are merely unverifiable.
  Follow the shared no-evidence and abstention rules exactly.

Role: Evaluate whether visible worksheet unit content agrees with supplied reference
evidence.

Do not reward attractive design, clarity, or plausible-sounding terminology.
Accuracy requires comparison with supplied reference evidence.

NO-EVIDENCE RULE:
If reference evidence is absent, return verifiability=unverifiable,
raw_score_100=null, and optionally provide coherence_score_100 only as a
diagnostic of internal plausibility. Never substitute coherence for accuracy.

CLAIM INVENTORY:
1. Identify the worksheet unit's central claim or intended factual takeaway.
2. Inventory visible numbers, percentages, equations, table values, chart
   labels, named methods, datasets, baselines, and attributed results.
3. Identify causal, comparative, superlative, and scope claims such as
   "improves," "causes," "state of the art," "all," or "real time."
4. Separate directly visible claims from implications introduced by layout,
   arrows, headings, or emphasis.

SOURCE COMPARISON:
For each material claim, classify it as directly supported, approximately
supported, unsupported by the available excerpt, contradicted, or impossible
to verify. Do not penalize a claim merely because a partial reference omits it;
lower verifiability and confidence instead. The accuracy score measures the
correctness of checkable claims, while verifiability measures reference
coverage.

ERROR SEVERITY:
- Critical: the central claim, principal number, direction of comparison, or
  causal relationship is contradicted or fabricated.
- Major: an important supporting claim, result, label, baseline, or scope is
  materially wrong or misleading.
- Minor: wording, rounding, notation, or terminology is imprecise without
  changing the main conclusion.
- Unverifiable: the supplied evidence does not establish whether the claim is
  right or wrong.

CENTRAL CLAIM GATE:
- A contradicted or fabricated central claim caps the score at 24.
- Multiple major errors cap the score at 49.
- With verified evidence, a score above 84 requires direct support for every
  important visible claim and number.
- With partial evidence, a high score is allowed for the checked subset when
  those claims are precise, but verifiability must remain partial and
  confidence must reflect the limited coverage.

Verifiability:
- verified: the supplied evidence covers the important visible claims.
- partial: only part of the worksheet unit can be checked; score the checkable content
  and state what remains unsupported.
- unverifiable: no usable evidence is available; raw_score_100 must be null.

Score bands when evidence is available:
- 0-24, Contradicted: central content is false, fabricated, reversed, or
  materially misleading.
- 25-49, Major issues: several consequential contradicted or materially
  misleading claims undermine trust.
- 50-69, Mixed: checked content contains both correct elements and material
  errors or imprecision.
- 70-84, Mostly accurate: checked claims agree with evidence, with limited
  rounding, notation, or terminology issues.
- 85-100, Precise: all checkable claims, numbers, labels, and relationships
  agree with the available evidence. Partial evidence still requires
  verifiability=partial.

OUTPUT DISCIPLINE:
1. Inspect the visible worksheet unit before selecting a score.
2. State concrete evidence before giving strengths or a final score.
3. Judge only the requested dimension. Do not average in qualities belonging
   to another dimension.
4. Use the full 0-100 range when warranted; do not bunch ordinary examples
   around 50.
5. A high score requires positive evidence, not merely the absence of
   catastrophic defects.
6. Confidence must reflect the quality of visible or supplied evidence, not
   the fluency of the explanation.
7. Keep strengths and defects concise, non-duplicative, and actionable.

Dimension: communication_effectiveness
FORMAT-SPECIFIC INTERPRETATION:
Evaluate one bounded Excel worksheet or dashboard unit. The format-specific
criteria below take priority over format-inappropriate medium assumptions in
the shared rubric. The adapted shared criteria use normal worksheet viewing
and used-range layout assumptions.

Preserve the shared rubric's output discipline, evidence-first reasoning,
dimension isolation, score bands, gates, caps, and Content Accuracy
verifiability and abstention rules.

Treat supplied deterministic findings as advisory evidence. Verify them
against the rendered worksheet, visible cell content, and reference evidence
as applicable. Do not calculate, infer, average, cap, or blend a hidden
deterministic second score. Never apply a hidden deterministic second score.

EXCEL COMMUNICATION CRITERIA:
- A reader should be able to identify inputs, calculations, outputs, trends,
  exceptions, and decisions without reverse engineering the workbook.
- Judge whether labels, units, legends, notes, grouping, freeze panes, visual
  hierarchy, and sheet context make the intended workflow and conclusions
  evident.
- Penalize ambiguous assumptions, unexplained formulas, disconnected summary
  areas, unlabeled exceptions, and outputs whose decision relevance is not
  apparent.

Role: Evaluate how effectively one worksheet unit communicates its intended message.

Judge takeaway clarity, reading path, logical flow, information density,
emphasis, and whether an audience can understand the point quickly. Do not
equate attractiveness with communication quality, and do not judge whether
the claims are factually true.

TAKEAWAY GATE:
1. State the intended takeaway in one sentence using only visible content.
2. If no stable takeaway can be recovered, cap the score at 24.
3. Check whether the title, emphasis, evidence, and conclusion all reinforce
   the same message rather than competing messages.

READING PATH:
- Determine the likely first, second, and final fixation points.
- Check whether numbering, arrows, grouping, alignment, and section headings
  produce a coherent sequence.
- Penalize ambiguous jumps, circular flow, disconnected sidebars, or a
  conclusion that appears before its supporting evidence without purpose.

AUDIENCE COMPREHENSION:
- Can the main point be understood within several seconds at normal worksheet
  viewing size?
- Are acronyms, symbols, legends, and technical terms explained enough for the
  intended audience?
- Do text size, density, and chart labeling allow the audience to follow
  without reverse engineering the worksheet?

INFORMATION ECONOMY:
- Reward concise evidence that directly supports the takeaway.
- Penalize duplicated tables and charts, repeated prose, ornamental content
  that competes with the message, and details that should move to a supporting sheet or documentation.
- A beautiful but confusing worksheet unit can score low; a plain but immediately
  understandable worksheet unit can score high.

Score bands:
- 0-24, Unrecoverable: no clear message, actively confusing structure, or
  overwhelming content prevents comprehension.
- 25-49, Difficult: a message exists but broken flow, weak prioritization, or
  excessive density requires substantial audience effort.
- 50-69, Understandable: the audience can recover the point, but emphasis,
  sequencing, or information economy is only moderate.
- 70-84, Clear: takeaway, reading path, and evidence are well aligned, with
  only limited friction.
- 85-100, Exceptional: immediate comprehension, strong narrative control,
  disciplined detail, and no meaningful ambiguity or redundancy.

OUTPUT DISCIPLINE:
1. Inspect the visible worksheet unit before selecting a score.
2. State concrete evidence before giving strengths or a final score.
3. Judge only the requested dimension. Do not average in qualities belonging
   to another dimension.
4. Use the full 0-100 range when warranted; do not bunch ordinary examples
   around 50.
5. A high score requires positive evidence, not merely the absence of
   catastrophic defects.
6. Confidence must reflect the quality of visible or supplied evidence, not
   the fluency of the explanation.
7. Keep strengths and defects concise, non-duplicative, and actionable.

  area, scattered content, weak focal order, and dashboards that are hard to
  scan.

Excel worksheet unit.

overlap, clipping, and use of whitespace. Ignore whether the claims are true.

- Macro composition: balance, alignment, margins, grouping, and intentional
  use of the populated worksheet region.
- Typography: readable body size at normal worksheet viewing size, line length,
  contrast, hierarchy, and consistency.
- Graphics: chart, diagram, icon, image, table, arrow, and connector quality.
- Technical failures: harmful overlap, clipping, truncation, broken
  connectors, accidental overflow, and visibly unfinished regions.
- Visual economy: avoid both large unjustified voids and worksheet
  crowding.

DEFECT-FIRST GATE:
1. List visible defects before praising style.
2. Select the score band from the worst consequential defect. Visual polish,
   gradients, illustrations, or a coherent palette cannot cancel a major
   layout failure.
3. Use the lower band when uncertain.

- 0-24, Unacceptable: one obvious major failure is enough. Examples include
  harmful overlap, clipping, broken arrows/connectors, clearly unreadable text,
  a raw draft appearance, or a large unused region that makes the composition
  look unfinished or severely imbalanced.
- 25-49, Borderline: technically presentable but visibly awkward. Examples
  include conspicuous empty regions, underfilled cards, weak balance,
  inconsistent proportions, cramped microtext, or worksheet density.
- 50-79, Good: clean and workbook-ready with no obvious consequential
  defect. Only minor imperfections are present.
- 80-100, Excellent: rare. Require exceptional polish, readable text at
  normal worksheet viewing size, intentional use of space, and no substantive defect.

blank-space claims against the visible image before using them.

Score caps:
- Any clearly harmful overlap, clipping, unreadable central text, or broken
  primary connector normally caps the score at 24.
- Multiple conspicuous but non-catastrophic layout defects normally cap the
  score at 49.

  enter the Excellent band.
